claims.text: A multiscale model that decouples phonon and electronic heat transport will predict HfNbTaTiZr thermal conductivity more accurately than prior analytical approaches.
The new model will reduce prediction error by at least 50%.
Relevant prior approaches assume defect-free crystals and use a single Debye temperature.
The relevant HfNbTaTiZr material typically contains approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
HfNbTaTiZr exhibits inherent lattice distortions arising from atomic-size and mass fluctuations.
Combining molecular dynamics, density-functional theory, and machine-learning regression can separately predict lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions.
Molecular dynamics can capture anharmonic phonon scattering caused by lattice distortions and oxygen defects in HfNbTaTiZr.
DFT-derived electron-scattering parameters can represent the electronic transport contribution in HfNbTaTiZr.
Below 200 K, the lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
The range up to 1200 K represents typical service conditions for the alloy.
Local lattice distortions alter force-constant fluctuations and thereby affect phonon scattering.
Oxygen-induced defect states alter force constants and electron relaxation times in HfNbTaTiZr.
Lattice distortion and nanostructural complexity can change HEA electronic transport through changes in carrier parameters and relaxation time.
Separately modeling anharmonic phonon dynamics and electron scattering avoids conflating lattice and electronic heat transport.
Treating a crystal as ideal and defect-free inherently conflates lattice and electronic thermal transport.
From 300 to 1200 K, HfNbTaTiZr containing about 1 wt.% oxygen has total thermal conductivity in the range 10–17 W/(K·m).
The model is applicable to HfNbTaTiZr with approximately 1 wt.% oxygen and typical lattice disorder, but may lose accuracy for substantially different impurities or defect populations.
Errors exceeding ±25% in either independently measured transport contribution, or an error reduction below 50% relative to traditional models, would falsify the hypothesis.
